before.label: History of science
before.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
before.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

before.label: Thomas Kuhn
before.description: Explains scientific development through normal science, disciplinary commitments, crises, and revolutions. Paradigms organize problems and standards of inquiry. Later sociologists adapt these arguments, sometimes in ways Kuhn disputes; this is not a universal law that all intellectual history moves through discrete paradigms. His preface acknowledges Koyré, Metzger, Maier and Fleck as distinct resources. The later distinction between shared disciplinary commitments and exemplary solutions makes “paradigm” more precise.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962; expanded second edition 1970). Distinguish his analysis of scientific communities from loose uses of paradigm to mean any school of historical writing. Read the 1962 preface alongside the 1969 postscript included in the second edition: sources of the argument and later clarification are different evidence.

after.label: Thomas Kuhn
after.description: Explains scientific development through normal science, disciplinary commitments, crises, and revolutions. Paradigms organize problems and standards of inquiry. Later sociologists adapt these arguments, sometimes in ways Kuhn disputes; this is not a universal law that all intellectual history moves through discrete paradigms. His preface acknowledges Koyré, Metzger, Maier and Fleck as distinct resources. The later distinction between shared disciplinary commitments and exemplary solutions makes “paradigm” more precise. In his 1970 exchange, Kuhn stresses substantial agreement with Popper while distinguishing tests of puzzle solutions from challenges to basic theory. Popper accepts that normal research exists but disputes its educational desirability; Lakatos later proposes appraisal of research programmes through novel predictions. Their accusations of irrationalism are criticisms of Kuhn, not his own stated position. Skinner, Dunn and deMause use Kuhn for different historical purposes.
